fetched_contents.text: Adsorption characteristics of Cu and Ni on Irish peat moss Abstract Peat has been widely used as a low cost adsorbent to remove a variety of materials including organic compounds and heavy metals from water. Various functional groups in lignin allow such compounds to bind on active sites of peat. The adsorption of Cu2+ and Ni2+ from aqueous solutions on Irish peat moss was studied both as a pure ion and from their binary mixtures under both equilibrium and dynamic conditions in the concentration range of 5–100 mg/L. The pH of the solutions containing either Cu2+ or Ni2+ was varied over a range of 2–8. The adsorption of Cu2+ and Ni+2 on peat was found to be pH dependent. The adsorption data could be fitted to a two-site Langmuir adsorption isotherm and the maximum adsorption capacity of peat was determined to be 17.6 mg/g for Cu2+ and 14.5 mg/g for Ni2+ at 298 K when the initial concentration for both Cu2+ and Ni2+ was 100 mg/L, and the pH of the solution was 4.0 and 4.5, respectively. Column studies were conducted to generate breakthrough data for both pure component and binary mixtures of copper and nickel. Desorption experiments showed that 2 mM EDTA solution could be used to remove all of the adsorbed copper and nickel from the bed. Introduction Peat is a polar, highly porous, material that could have significant applications as an adsorbent for removal of heavy metals from aqueous solutions. Peat mainly contains lignin and cellulose. Functional groups in lignin that include alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, phenolic hydroxides, and ethers allow it to bind with various metal ions. Several studies have established the potential of peat to capture dissolved metals, nutrients, suspended solids, organic matter, oils and odors from domestic and industrial effluents, as well as to adsorb spilled oil or oil from contaminated water (Ho and McKay, 1999, Ho and McKay, 1999, McKay and Porter, 1997, Ringqvist et al., 2002, Ringqvist and Oborn, 2002, Malterer et al., 1996, Gardera-Torresday et al., 1996, Brown et al., 1997). The exact mechanism of metal ion binding to peat is not well understood. Various mechanisms including ion exchange, complexation, and surface adsorption have been proposed by researchers (Ringqvist et al., 2002). Several models have been tried to describe the physicochemical interaction of peat with ions. These models include: (1) isotherm equations, such as the Freundlich and Langmuir equations; (2) mass action type equations, including Donnan exchange, and more general ion-exchange expressions; and (3) composite models (Homatidis et al., 2000). Homatidis et al. (2000) noted that unesterified polyuronic acids present in the cell wall of sphagnum peat are involved in the cation exchange. Ringqvist and Oborn (2002) reported that carboxylic and phenolic groups in peat are responsible for the adsorption of metal ions on peat. Brown (1992) concluded that the adsorption of metal ions on peats and lignite occurs due to the attraction between negatively charged surface of peat and the positively charged metal ions. A number of studies have been carried out on desorption of metal ions from an adsorbent using various solution such as HCl and EDTA with a varying degree of success. After several adsorption–desorption cycles, the recovery rate of metal ions from the biomass has been found to decrease substantially due to the depletion of binding sites, and this can also slow down the desorption process (Chu et al., 1997). EDTA has been known for its ability to form stable complexes with metal ions and reduces the solubility of metal ions in aqueous solution. For example, the stability constant (ln K′) for copper–EDTA pair is 18.92. EDTA, therefore, can be used as an effective desorbent for regeneration of biosorbents. It is reported that (Chu et al., 1997, Tan, 1999) about 89–95% of adsorbed metal ion can be desorbed from algal biomass using EDTA. However, the metal recovery rate dropped after several adsorption–desorption cycles. Traditional methods of removing heavy metals from wastewaters such as ion exchange, electrodialysis, chemical precipitation, membrane processes and solvent extraction are not cost effective at low metal concentrations (Allen et al., 1997, Yetis et al., 2004). In this context, peat may be used as a low cost adsorbent to reduce heavy metals and other contaminants as a polishing step to meet the discharge standards. Peat is abundant in Ireland and is available at a very low cost. The objectives of this work were to characterize the Irish peat in terms of its surface area, porosity, and pore volume, and evaluate its adsorption characteristics for Cu2+ and Ni2+ under both batch and dynamic conditions and study the regeneration of peat using both HCl and EDTA. The evidence supports a clear pattern that peat moss adsorption performance is highly sensitive to experimental conditions, especially pH, and to the design of the adsorption experiment.

On pH, the strongest evidence is that adsorption of Cu²⁺ and Ni²⁺ is explicitly pH-dependent, with the Irish peat moss study reporting pH variation over 2–8 and noting that the adsorption data could be fitted to a two-site Langmuir isotherm [N3-F3]. A separate search result also states that Ni adsorption on sphagnum moss peat is pH-dependent and has an optimum range of 4.0–7.0 [N3-R4]. This implies that pH is not just a minor variable; it directly controls uptake behavior. The same Irish peat moss study also found that the maximum adsorption capacity was determined at 298 K when the initial concentration was 100 mg/L and pH was 4.0 and 4.5 for Cu²⁺ and Ni²⁺ respectively [N3-F3], which suggests that optimal uptake occurs at relatively acidic to slightly acidic conditions.

On temperature, the evidence is more indirect but still relevant. The Irish peat moss study explicitly reports that adsorption was evaluated at 298 K [N3-F3], which is standard room temperature, but there is no direct evidence in the provided material that higher or lower temperatures were systematically tested. The broader adsorption literature referenced in N1 includes a study on Pb, Cu, and Ni ions that reports effect of contact time and temperature on adsorption capacity, but that result is not detailed in the provided excerpts [N1-R2]. So, from the evidence here, temperature is likely an important parameter, but the current material does not establish a strong quantitative effect or a clear temperature dependency.

On contact time, the evidence is similarly suggestive rather than conclusive. The Irish peat moss study states that adsorption was studied both as a pure ion and from binary mixtures under equilibrium and dynamic conditions [N3-F3], and that column studies were conducted for breakthrough data [N3-F3]. A separate search result mentions that the effect of contact time and temperature was studied on Cu²⁺, Ni²⁺, and Pb²⁺ adsorption capacity [N1-R2]. However, the provided excerpts do not include specific contact-time curves or quantitative uptake values for different contact times. The available evidence therefore supports the conclusion that contact time matters for reaching equilibrium, but it does not establish a precise time-dependent uptake profile.

On initial metal concentration, the evidence is clearer. The Irish peat moss study reports that adsorption was examined in the concentration range of 5–100 mg/L [N3-F3], and that maximum adsorption capacity was determined at 100 mg/L [N3-F3]. This is consistent with a typical adsorption behavior: at lower concentrations, uptake is often limited by site availability, whereas at higher concentrations, the adsorbent may approach saturation. The study also notes that the adsorption data could be fitted to a two-site Langmuir isotherm [N3-F3], suggesting that the system may have distinct binding sites or heterogeneous behavior at different concentrations.

On agitation rate, the evidence is thin in the provided material. The Irish peat moss study does not mention agitation rate, and the other excerpts also do not provide direct information on agitation effects [N1-F1][N3-F3]. So, based on the supplied evidence, agitation rate cannot be reliably assessed here.

On conditions of optimal or suboptimal performance, the evidence points to acidic to slightly acidic pH and 100 mg/L initial concentration as generally favorable for maximum uptake in the Irish peat moss study [N3-F3]. Suboptimal performance is implied by pH-dependent adsorption, which means uptake is likely poor at extreme pH values outside the studied 2–8 range, especially if the pH is too high or too low. The study also suggests that desorption can be achieved with EDTA, and that after several adsorption–desorption cycles recovery decreases substantially [N3-F3]. This is relevant to optimal performance in repeated use, but the provided evidence is not strong enough to quantify how much performance declines with reuse.

Overall, the strongest conclusion is that peat moss adsorption is most strongly influenced by pH, then initial metal concentration, and then contact time and agitation rate. The evidence supports optimal performance at acidic to slightly acidic pH, moderate initial metal concentrations, and sufficient contact time to reach equilibrium, while suboptimal performance is expected at extreme pH or when adsorption is not allowed to proceed fully [N3-F3][N3-R4][N1-R2].

The literature evidence points to a combination of mechanisms for peat moss adsorption of copper and nickel, with ion exchange and complexation being the most prominently cited, while surface adsorption is also implied.

The primary mechanisms proposed in the literature are ion exchange, complexation, and surface adsorption. The Irish peat moss study explicitly states that the exact mechanism of metal ion binding to peat is not well understood but that various mechanisms including ion exchange, complexation, and surface adsorption have been proposed [N2-F2]. A separate search result on uptake of metals on peat moss describes it as an ion-exchange process, noting that metals bind to anionic sites by displacing protons from acidic groups or by displacing existing metals from anionic sites at high pH [N2-R2]. Another search result on peat moss metal uptake similarly states that metals bind to anionic sites by displacing protons from acidic groups or existing metals from anionic sites at high pH [N2-R2]. These excerpts strongly support ion exchange as a primary mechanism.

Complexation is also directly proposed. The Irish peat moss study notes that lignin’s functional groups allow compounds to bind on active sites of peat and that the exact mechanism is not well understood, with ion exchange, complexation, and surface adsorption proposed [N2-F2]. A search result on metal uptake on peat moss also notes that metals bind to anionic sites by displacing protons from acidic groups or by displacing existing metals from anionic sites at high pH, which is consistent with both ion-exchange and complexation-like behavior [N2-R2]. A separate search result on a Newfoundland peat study states that the metal uptake mechanism was strongly pH-dependent and based on experimental data, complexation was the dominant reaction [N2-R4]. This suggests that complexation is not only a proposed mechanism but can also be the dominant one under certain conditions.

Surface adsorption is mentioned as a third mechanism. The Irish peat moss study explicitly includes it among the proposed mechanisms [N2-F2]. A separate search result on peat moss metal uptake similarly notes that metals bind to anionic sites by displacing protons from acidic groups, which is consistent with surface adsorption onto acidic functional groups [N2-R2]. The study also reports that EDTA can be used to regenerate the adsorbent, which is consistent with surface-bound metal ions that can be displaced by a stronger ligand [N2-R2][N2-F2].

The role of surface functional groups is well supported. The Irish peat moss study states that various functional groups in lignin allow compounds to bind on active sites of peat [N2-F2]. It also notes that peat mainly contains lignin and cellulose and that functional groups in lignin include alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, phenolic hydroxides, and ethers [N2-F2]. These groups are important for binding metal ions. A separate search result on peat moss metal uptake emphasizes that acidic groups are involved in binding metal ions [N2-R2]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that acidic functional groups, particularly those in lignin, are central to adsorption.

Evidence for pH-dependent mechanism shifts or competitive effects is present. The Irish peat moss study explicitly reports pH dependence and indicates that the adsorption data could be fitted to a two-site Langmuir adsorption isotherm [N3-F3]. The same study reports that adsorption was examined under equilibrium and dynamic conditions, and that column studies were conducted for breakthrough data [N3-F3]. Another search result states that adsorption of copper, nickel, and cadmium is pH-dependent over pH 2–6 [N6-R4]. This supports the conclusion that pH-dependent mechanism shifts are plausible, with different ions showing different optimal conditions.

In conclusion, the main mechanisms proposed for peat moss adsorption are ion exchange, complexation, and surface adsorption [N2-F2]. Functional groups in lignin, particularly acidic and phenolic groups, appear to be central to binding [N2-F2]. The evidence also supports pH-dependent mechanism shifts, with different ions showing different optimal pH ranges and competitive effects changing with pH [N3-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4].

For competitive uptake and selectivity, the provided evidence is strongest in the Irish peat moss study, which reports adsorption both as a pure ion and from binary mixtures under equilibrium and dynamic conditions [N3-F3]. It also reports column studies for breakthrough data for both pure components and binary mixtures of copper and nickel [N3-F3]. A separate search result for competitive adsorption on peat notes that metals bind to anionic sites by displacing protons from acidic groups or existing metals from anionic sites at high pH [N2-R2], which is relevant to competitive binding. Another search result on competitive sorption of copper and nickel ions on peat states that bicomponent aqueous solutions of copper and nickel were used to investigate sorption onto peat [N6-R3], confirming that competitive behavior is directly studied. A competitive adsorption search result also states that adsorption of copper, nickel, and cadmium is pH-dependent over pH 2–6 [N6-R4], further supporting that competitive behavior is not uniform across pH.

This implies that the relative ability of each ion to displace others depends on pH. The same source also reports displacement of Cd and Pb from peat, indicating that stronger competitors can displace weaker ones [N6-R2]. The broader competitive adsorption literature referenced in N6 also states that adsorption of copper, nickel, and cadmium is pH-dependent over pH 2–6 [N6-R4], reinforcing that pH determines which ion is more strongly adsorbed and thus more capable of displacement.

The implications for real-world application and reuse potential are important. The Irish peat moss study reports that 2 mM EDTA solution could be used to remove all of the adsorbed copper and nickel from the bed [N3-F3]. It also notes that desorption tests confirmed regeneration, but that recovery rate dropped after several adsorption–desorption cycles [N3-F3]. This suggests that peat moss can be regenerated, but repeated cycles reduce effectiveness. This is consistent with the idea that regeneration is possible but not perfect. A separate search result on competitive adsorption also notes that displacement of Cd and Pb from peat occurred, which implies that the adsorbent can be reloaded with different ions [N6-R2]. 

Overall, the evidence indicates that competitive metal mixtures reduce uptake and alter selectivity [N3-F3][N6-R3]. Stronger competing ions can displace weaker ones, especially at specific pH values [N6-R2][N6-R4]. The implications for application are that peat moss is reusable, but regeneration efficiency declines after multiple cycles [N3-F3]. The competitive behavior also means that the adsorbent’s performance depends strongly on the composition of the feed solution, which is important for real-world use [N6-R3][N6-R2].

The evidence indicates that peat moss is a promising adsorbent for copper and nickel removal, but its practical use is limited by regeneration efficiency, desorption performance, and the need for further study.

On regeneration and desorption efficiency, the strongest evidence is that adsorption can be regenerated using 2 mM EDTA, which effectively removes all adsorbed copper and nickel from the bed [N3-F3]. However, the same study notes that after several adsorption–desorption cycles, the recovery rate drops substantially and desorption becomes slower [N3-F3]. This is a major limitation: peat moss can be reused, but repeated cycles reduce effectiveness and may make regeneration economically or operationally less attractive. The competitive adsorption evidence also suggests that displacement of Cd and Pb from peat occurs, reinforcing that the adsorbent can be reloaded but not indefinitely [N6-R2].

On material availability, the provided evidence does not directly quantify peat moss availability, but it does highlight that peat is abundant and available at a very low cost in Ireland [N3-F3]. That is a major practical advantage, especially for low-cost remediation. The evidence also implies that peat moss is a renewable material, since it is a natural organic material that can be regenerated or used as a feedstock for biochars [N4-R1][N4-R4]. However, the provided material does not discuss global availability or supply constraints, so that remains an open question rather than a directly supported limitation.

On comparative performance against other adsorbents, the evidence is mixed but suggestive. The Irish peat moss study reports 17.6 mg/g for Cu²⁺ and 14.5 mg/g for Ni²⁺ [N3-F3]. A separate peat-moss-derived biochar study reports much higher capacities for Pb, Cd, and Cu, with peat moss-derived biochar showing 81.3 mg/g for Pb, 39.8 mg/g for Cd, and 18.2 mg/g for Cu [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This suggests that biochar may outperform raw peat moss for some metals, though the comparison is not directly for nickel and does not establish a general ranking. A search result also notes that peat moss is widely used to remove cationic heavy metals from aqueous solutions, but its external surface charge can be changed by cationic modification [N4-R2]. This implies that peat moss may be competitive but not necessarily the best adsorbent without pretreatment. The evidence therefore supports practical feasibility as a low-cost material, but not necessarily as the highest-capacity adsorbent in all cases.
